vA2=5gLv_A^2 = 5gL

Ratio of Kinetic Energies

The function \(f(x)=2 x+3(x)^{\frac{2}{3}}, x \in R\), has

 

[JEE Main 2024, 29 Jan (Shift 2)]
options: exactly two points of local maxima and exactly one point of local minima
exactly one point of local maxima and exactly one point of local minima
exactly one point of local maxima and no point of local minima
exactly one point of local minima and no point of local maxima
questions.explanation:
Given \(f(x)=2x+3x^{2/3}\)

For \(x\ne0\)

\(f'(x)=2+2x^{-1/3}=2\left(1+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]{x}}\right)\)

Setting \(f'(x)=0\), we get

\(\sqrt[3]{x}=-1\), so \(x=-1\)

For \(x<-1\), \(f'(x)>0\)

For \(-1<x<0\), \(f'(x)<0\)

Therefore, \(f\) changes from increasing to decreasing at \(x=-1\),

so \(x=-1\) is a point of local maximum

The derivative is not defined at \(x=0\), 

For \(x>0\), \(f(x)=x^{2/3}(2x^{1/3}+3)>0=f(0)\)

For \(x<0\), let \(u=\sqrt[3]{-x}>0\)

Then \(x=-u^3\), \(x^{2/3}=u^2\),

and \(f(x)=u^2(3-2u)\)

For \(x\) sufficiently close to \(0\),

\(u<\dfrac{3}{2}\), so \(f(x)>0=f(0)\)

Therefore, \(x=0\) is a point of local minimum.

For \(x>0\), \(f'(x)>0\),

so there are no further local extrema.

Hence there is exactly one point of local maximum and exactly one point of local minimum.

Thus \(I=\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(\cos x-\sin x)\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}(\sin x-\cos x)\,dx\).

Now \(\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(\cos x-\sin x)\,dx=\left[\sin x+\cos x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\).

So \(\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(\cos x-\sin x)\,dx=\sqrt2-\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\).

Also \(\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}(\sin x-\cos x)\,dx=\left[-\cos x-\sin x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\).

So \(\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}(\sin x-\cos x)\,dx=\sqrt2-\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\).

Therefore \(I=2\sqrt2-(1+\sqrt3)\).

Thus \(I=-1+2\sqrt2-\sqrt3\).

Comparing with \(\alpha+\beta\sqrt2+\gamma\sqrt3\), we get \(\alpha=-1\), \(\beta=2\), and \(\gamma=-1\).

Hence \(3\alpha+4\beta-\gamma=3(-1)+4(2)-(-1)\).

Therefore \(3\alpha+4\beta-\gamma=-3+8+1=6\).

questions.question:
Let \(P(\alpha, \beta)\) be a point on the parabola \(y^2=4 x\). If \(P\) also lies on the chord of the parabola \(x^2=8 y\) whose mid point is \(\left(1, \frac{5}{4}\right)\), then \((\alpha-28)(\beta-8)\) is equal to _____ .

 

[JEE Main 2024, 29 Jan (Shift 2)]
questions.explanation:
The chord of the parabola \(x^2=8y\) whose midpoint is \(\left(1,\dfrac{5}{4}\right)\) is obtained from \(T=S_1\).

For \(x^2=8y\), \(S=x^2-8y\).

At the midpoint,

\(S_1=1^2-8\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right)=-9\)

The chord is

\(x(1)-4\left(y+\dfrac{5}{4}\right)=-9\)

\(x-4y+4=0\)

\(\therefore \alpha=4\beta-4\)

Also, \(P(\alpha,\beta)\) lies on \(y^2=4x\).

\(\beta^2=4\alpha\)

\(\beta^2=4(4\beta-4)\)

\(\beta^2-16\beta+16=0\)

\(\beta=8\pm4\sqrt{3}\)

\(\alpha=4\beta-4=28\pm16\sqrt{3}\)

The signs are corresponding.

\((\alpha-28)(\beta-8)=(\pm16\sqrt{3})(\pm4\sqrt{3})=192\)

\(\therefore\) the required value is \(192\).

Then \(\overrightarrow{O M} \cdot \overrightarrow{O N}\) is equal to ________ .

\(\mathrm{L}_1: \frac{\mathrm{x}-5}{4}=\frac{\mathrm{y}-4}{1}=\frac{\mathrm{z}-5}{3}=\lambda\)

\(\mathrm{M}(4 \lambda+5, \lambda+4,3 \lambda+5)\)

\(\operatorname{dr's}(12,5,9)=\mathrm{b}_2\)
\(\mathrm{N}(12 \mu-8,5 \mu-2,9 \mu-11)\)
\(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{MN}}=(4 \lambda-12 \mu+13, \lambda-5 \mu+6, 3 \lambda-9 \mu+16) \quad \ldots .(1)\)

Now

\(\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}_1 \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}_2 & =\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathrm{i}} & \hat{\mathrm{j}} & \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\
4 & 1 & 3 \\
12 & 5 & 9
\end{array}\right|=-6 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+8 \hat{\mathrm{k}} \ldots .(2)
\end{aligned}\)

From equation (1) and (2)

\(\therefore \frac{4 \lambda-12 \mu+13}{-6}=\frac{\lambda-5 \mu+6}{0}=\frac{3 \lambda-9 \mu+16}{8}\)

taking I and II

\(\lambda-5 \mu+6=0 \quad \ldots .(3)\)

taking I and III

\(\lambda-3 \mu+4=0 \quad \ldots .(4)\)

From equation (3) and (4), we get
\(\lambda=-1, \mu=1\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{M}(1,3,2)\) and \(\mathrm{N}(4,3,-2)\)
\(\therefore \overrightarrow{\mathrm{OM}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{ON}}=4+9-4=9\)

questions.question:
Let the slope of the line \(45 x+5 y+3=0\) be \(27 r_1+\frac{9 r_2}{2}\) for some \(r_1, r_2 \in R\). Then \(\lim _{x \rightarrow 3}\left(\int_3^x \frac{8 t^2}{\frac{3 r_2 x}{2}-r_2 x^2-r_1 x^3-3 x} d t\right)\) is equal to _________

 

[JEE Main 2024, 29 Jan (Shift 2)]
questions.explanation:
The line is \(45x+5y+3=0\).

Writing it as \(y=-9x-\dfrac{3}{5}\), its slope is \(-9\).

The question gives the slope as \(27r_1+\dfrac{9r_2}{2}\).

Therefore, \(27r_1+\dfrac{9r_2}{2}=-9\).

Let \(D(x)=\dfrac{3r_2x}{2}-r_2x^2-r_1x^3-3x\).

Since the denominator does not depend on the integration variable \(t\), the given expression is \(\dfrac{\displaystyle\int_{3}^{x}8t^2dt}{D(x)}\).

Now \(\displaystyle\int_{3}^{x}8t^2dt=\dfrac{8}{3}(x^3-27)\).

At \(x=3\), the numerator is \(0\).

Also, \(D(3)=\dfrac{9r_2}{2}-9r_2-27r_1-9=-\left(27r_1+\dfrac{9r_2}{2}+9\right)=0\).

Thus, the limit has the form \(\dfrac{0}{0}\), so L'Hospital's rule can be applied.

The derivative of the numerator is \(8x^2\).

Also, \(D'(x)=\dfrac{3r_2}{2}-2r_2x-3r_1x^2-3\).

Therefore, \(D'(3)=\dfrac{3r_2}{2}-6r_2-27r_1-3=-\left(27r_1+\dfrac{9r_2}{2}\right)-3\).

Using \(27r_1+\dfrac{9r_2}{2}=-9\), we get \(D'(3)=9-3=6\).

Hence, the required limit is \(\dfrac{8\cdot3^2}{6}=\dfrac{72}{6}=12\).
